title: Your first PHP page
summary: What the server does with a .php file, and how to print something.

blocks.html:
A .php file is not sent to the browser. The server reads it, runs the parts inside <?php ?>, and sends whatever the script printed. The visitor never sees your source code — only the result.

That is the whole idea of a server-side language: the page is built fresh on every request, by code that runs on the server.

blocks.title: one request, start to finish
blocks.ascii:
browser                        server

  GET /index.php  ----------->  Apache
                                  |
                                  v
                               PHP interpreter
                                  |  runs index.php
                                  v
  HTML  <---------------------  the page it printed

  The PHP source never leaves the server.

blocks.html:
echo writes to the response body. Nothing is added around it: no newline, no HTML, no quotes. What you print is what arrives.

Anything outside the PHP tags is copied to the output untouched. That is how a PHP file can be mostly HTML with a few dynamic islands.

These snippets run as standalone scripts, which is why they print plain text. In this repository the same code runs inside Apache: docker compose up -d, then open http://localhost. The file public/index.php is the entry point, and it includes one exercise at a time.
echo accepts several comma-separated values and prints them in order, with nothing between them — not even a space. Add the space yourself, or use . to concatenate strings into one value.
The dot is not optional. "Hello" "world" is a syntax error, because two values in a row mean nothing to PHP — you must say how they combine.

blocks.title: comments
blocks.code:
<?php

// A line comment runs to the end of the line.
# This style works too, but // is the convention. /* This one spans lines. */

echo "comments are free";

quiz.q: What does the browser receive when it requests a .php file?
quiz.why: The server executes the file and sends only the output. The source stays on the server.

quiz.q: Which of these prints ab with no space?
quiz.why: Comma-separated echo arguments and dot concatenation both produce ab. The comma form prints each value in turn; the dot form builds one string first.

quiz.q: What is printed by a file that contains only HTML, with no <?php tag?
options: An error about a missing tag
quiz.why: Text outside PHP tags is sent as-is. A .php file with no PHP in it is a perfectly valid static page.

exercise.brief: Print exactly two lines. The first is the word PHP. The second is sum: followed by the result of 2 + 2.
exercise.hint: Each echo writes one line if you end it with \n. The value of 2 + 2 can be printed directly: echo "sum: ", 2 + 2, "\n";
